title: Brit monster hunter commits 'career suicide' after slamming 'Bigfoot religion'
excerpt: British paranormal host Andy McGrath lifts the lid on the 'Bigfoot religion' after a newly unearthed rehearsal tape exposed the iconic 1967 footage as fake
content:
A British monster hunter has lifted the lid on the bitter civil war tearing apart the "Bigfoot religion" after the world's most famous ape-man footage was exposed as a hoax. Paranormal investigator and Weird Britain host Andy McGrath admits that he's committing 'career suicide' by speaking out against the iconic 1967 Patterson–Gimlin film.

The film, which shows 'Bigfoot' clearly walking through a forest, was seen as the moment that helped introduce a whole new group of people to the hairy ape. But the community was thrown into disarray with the release of explosive documentary Capturing Bigfoot, which unearthed a vault rehearsal tape of the legendary Sasquatch suit from a year earlier alongside a confession from filmmaker Roger Patterson's late widow, Patricia.

It left die-hard fans scambling to dismiss accusations of fakery.

"People are very invested in it, and some of this investiture sometimes takes the form of a kind of religiosity," Andy told the Daily Star.

‌

"Lots of people know Bob Gimlin, the surviving member from the Patterson–Gimlin film, and have been essentially screeching from the rooftops that this film must not be watched - that it's some sort of AI, a fit-up, a money grab."

Andy, author of Beasts of Britain and Hairy Humanoids, admitted the footage first drew him into the genre as a teenager.

Even top US anthropologist Dr Jeff Meldrum "went white" on camera when shown the rehearsal footage, Andy noted.

‌

However, he pointed to an overlooked pre-shoot photo showing Gimlin in a wig and face paint posing as an "Indian tracker" as proof the expedition was staged from day one.

"In view of what I've seen, my view is that it is a [fake] and there can be no other possibility," he said. "Some people have launched book careers off of it, they've made their living from it, and now that's over.

"I didn't really mention my doubts before because it's sort of career suicide to go against it in that genre."

‌

Despite branding the film a hoax, Andy refused to attack surviving cameraman Gimlin, now 94, insisting the cowboy was likely trapped in a ruse that spiralled out of control.

"Good people sometimes do bad things, and there isn't always a way out," he said. "Would I have the courage after six decades, at 94 years old, to say, 'Oh, by the way, everyone'? I don't think I would personally."

Closer to home, Andy believes the fallout exposes a stark divide between America's "mercenary" Bigfoot industry, where groups flog plaster footprint casts, and Brits who keep quiet about sightings for fear of becoming a laughing stock.

‌

"What I discovered about most British reports is they're nearly all second or third-hand," he said. "If you see Nessie, that's a badge of honour - everybody thinks it's a lot of fun.

"Whereas if you go into your workplace saying you saw a Yeti in the woods, they're going to say, 'I'm not sure if [he's] the right guy for this next promotion'."

While Britain has centuries-old carvings of hairy "Wodewose" wild men on medieval churches and tapestries, Andy says modern UK sightings have exploded thanks to American TV shows like Finding Bigfoot.

‌

Comparing the phenomenon to a Derren Brown illusion, he argues pop culture plants a mental image in witnesses' heads until they genuinely believe they have spotted an ape-man in the British countryside.

"We're dealing with modern folklore happening in real time that exists in the collective consciousness of people," he said. "This folklore has been planted and replanted in our cultural mind for generations."
